transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-28 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Alex (BrightEdge Head ML Infra), Priya (Platform Eng), Daniel (CTO)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we're going to dive into autoscaling and capacity planning, we wanted to make sure we cover burst policies, queueing models, reserved GPUs, and any constraints you have in your VPC/on-prem setups. Ethan will run through the technical bits.
[00:18] Alex: yep, thanks. quick context: we're running a multi-tenant inferencing layer in k8s today, it's kinda re-used from our training infra, and we're seeing big tail latencies during batch job windows and business spikes. main ask: keep 95th under 500ms for chat completions and control monthly cost.
[00:35] Ethan: cool. just to confirm, are most of your requests short chat turns or long-document generations? that affects batch sizes and KV cache behavior.
[00:44] Priya: 80% short chat, 20% long context summarizations - the long ones go up to 2k tokens occasionally. we also have a few nightly bulk pipelines.
[01:02] Ethan: got it. so two main patterns - low-latency short requests where batching helps up to a point but hurts p95 if you wait too long; and long contexts where KV cache memory and sequence length dominate throughput.
[01:18] Daniel: and we have to run inside our VPC, sometimes on-prem racks for compliance. so network egress and KMS integration are must-haves.
[01:28] Maya: yes, Redwood Private supports customer-managed networking and KMS/HSM integrations - we'll include the integration notes.
[01:35] [00:60] Ethan: first, about reserved GPUs vs burst: reserved GPUs give you predictable baseline throughput - you pin N slots, each slot has a model instance and memory for KV cache. burst lets you temporarily spin up more capacity in higher tiers, but there is cold-start and warm-up effects. so you get lower tail latency with enough reserved capacity; burst reduces cost by not keeping everything warm.
[02:05] Alex: can you quantify the warm-up? like if we get a spike, how long till the new slot is ready and KV cache is useful?
[02:15] Ethan: depends on model and quantization. for a 13B model in q4/h8 quant, cold start 20-45s to load and warm KV cache; with compiled kernels and pre-warmed images it can be ~10-20s. but the KV cache effectiveness grows as sessions repeat - first few requests miss cache. for chat latency-sensitive paths, we often recommend a hybrid: maintain reserved slots sized for typical 95th traffic, plus burst for rare peaks.
[02:45] Priya: that 20-45s is... rough for us - we can't tolerate that for customer-facing spikes.
[02:52] Ethan: understood. you can mitigate by faster slot reuse and smarter routing - e.g., keep a small pool of warm burst nodes in the same AZ as reserved ones (warm standby), or use fast autoscale cooldowns and prefetching for priority customers. also, continuous batching on the runtime can accept single requests but still use optimized kernels to reduce per-token overhead.
[03:18] [03:30] Alex: talk through queueing model - if we have 50 RPS baseline and 200 RPS spike, what happens to p95? do you queue and route or drop?
[03:38] Ethan: Redwood's routing has two levers: queueing with SLO-aware admission, and priority routing. if queue depth grows, we can route non-critical requests to cheaper model variants or a lower tier with longer latency SLOs. For hard SLOs, you size reserved capacity so that expected spikes are absorbed by in-provisioned capacity; otherwise you accept some queueing and add burst to reduce p95. we also instrument per-request TTLs and queue thresholds.
[04:05] Daniel: curious about the math - are you modeling with M/M/c or something more complex?
[04:12] Ethan: good question - we use a mixture: baseline M/G/1 approximations for single-slot behavior and M/M/c for homogeneous pools, but for realistic traffic we fold in empirical latency percentiles from your traces, and simulate with your inter-arrival and size distributions. that's why we asked for traffic traces.
[04:35] Alex: ok we'll share.
[04:38] [05:00] Priya: KV cache - is it per-slot or shared? what's the hit-rate we can expect for chat?
[05:05] Ethan: KV cache is per-model-instance (per-slot) because it's resident GPU memory. Hit rate depends on session stickiness - if you route the same conversation to the same slot you get very high hits. For multi-tenant setups without affinity, hit-rate drops. Typical chat workloads with sticky sessions see 60-90% KV hit for repeating prefixes; ad-hoc sessions are lower ~20-40%. You can improve by routing policies that pin or route by user/session-id.
[05:40] Alex: we do session affinity at LB layer today; would be good to keep that.
[05:44] Ethan: perfect. that pairs well with reserved slots - keeps KV warm and reduces token cost.
[05:50] [06:00] Maya: can you talk quantization tradeoffs? our lab models are sensitive to quality.
[06:06] Ethan: absolutely. quantization (e.g., 4-bit vs 8-bit) reduces memory and increases throughput, but you may see small accuracy/regression on worst-case prompts - especially for generation fidelity in long-context summarization. Redwood Optimize recommends model-specific quant profiles: for chat-heavy you'd use aggressive quant on lower-criticality models, and maintain higher-precision variants for quality-critical routes. Also the runtime can fallback to higher precision for flagged prompts.
[06:36] Priya: is switching between quantized variants live? how does rollout work?
[06:40] Ethan: yes, rollout supports canary and A/B with automatic fallback. it does require loading multiple variants into pools or using fast model switch where supported; there's a memory/slot cost.
[06:50] [07:00] Alex: about batching - we want to maximize throughput but keep p95 under 500ms. how to pick batch window and max batch size?
[07:07] Ethan: it's a tradeoff. small batch windows reduce queuing latency, while larger batches improve GPU utilization. We recommend adaptive batching: start with a 8-12ms short delay to collect small batches for low latency, and allow larger batches during non-peak. Your 95th requirement suggests favoring shorter windows and reserved capacity to keep utilization high without excessive batching. We can run bench tests with your request shape.
[07:38] [08:00] Daniel: network - our Private deployment will be VPC-only, with KMS. any special notes for on-prem?
[08:06] Ethan: for on-prem the main concerns are image registry access, node provisioning speed, and network bandwidth for model artifacts. If you want very low burst cold-start, pre-pull images to standby nodes and keep model files on local NVMe. For KMS, Redwood supports customer-managed keys and HSM integrations; we'll include the SOC2/ISO docs.
[08:34] Priya: good. also we want RBAC and audit logs for every inference.
[08:38] Maya: Redwood Console has per-route and per-token tracing with audit logs and retention options - we'll attach the docs.
[08:45] [09:00] Alex: follow-up on sizing: can you give a quick worked example? say a 13B model q4 with avg latency 40ms per token and average response length 40 tokens for chat, 95th latency goal 500ms, baseline 50 RPS, spikes 200 RPS.
[09:15] Ethan: rough calc: per-request compute time = 40ms * 40 tokens = 1600ms of GPU time, but GPU throughput and batching pipelining reduce wall time. On a well-optimized GPU with batching, one slot might handle ~20-30 concurrent small chats (this is finger-in-the-air; we'll run bench). So for baseline 50 RPS you might need 2-3 slots reserved; spikes to 200 RPS might need 8-10 slots unless you use larger batches and accept slightly higher p95. We'll provide a sizing worksheet with simulated queues.
[09:56] Alex: ok that's helpful.
[10:00] [10:30] Priya: storage - do KV caches persist across container restarts?
[10:33] Ethan: KV lives in GPU memory; unless you use an external snapshot mechanism it's ephemeral. For conversation continuity you either keep affinity or persist conversation context in user-prefetch storage and warm the model on reconnect. Persisting full KV is expensive.
[10:50] Daniel: any suggestions to reduce per-token cost?
[10:54] Ethan: prefix caching, reranking on cheaper models, and small-context prompts for repeated system messages. Also you can offload embeddings/rerank to CPU-backed services for some workflows. Redwood Optimize will suggest quantization and batching profiles per-route.
[11:12] [12:00] Maya: ok, let's talk burst policy design: we typically see spikes for 10-30 minutes during product launches. Alex, what's your spike profile?
[12:20] Alex: usually 15-minute spikes with sudden ramp; not sustained more than 30 minutes.
[12:28] Ethan: for that pattern, recommended policy: maintain reserved capacity for baseline + short-term warm standby (1-2 nodes pre-warmed but idle), configure fast autoscale with pre-pulled images, and a burst cap that prevents overprovisioning beyond budget. Also set SLO-aware admission: non-critical background requests can be deprioritized when queue grows.
[12:52] Priya: how do we cost that - reserved nodes cost monthly, warm standby are cheaper but still billed?
[12:59] Ethan: reserved committed capacity is billed at discounted rate. Warm standby nodes that are idle but kept warm will still be billed; burst that uses on-demand or spot will vary. We'll send a cost example.
[13:14] [13:30] Alex: can Redwood autoscaler integrate with our internal scheduler or do we need to use Redwood's control plane?
[13:38] Ethan: for Private deployments you can run Redwood control plane on customer network or integrate via API. We can expose autoscale hooks for your scheduler or let Redwood manage node counts. Many customers prefer Redwood-managed autoscaling to get the SLO-aware routing logic.
[13:58] Daniel: we need to be able to audit every scale event.
[14:02] Maya: all scale events and routing decisions are logged in the console and can be shipped to your SIEM. we'll include log sample.
[14:12] [14:30] Priya: any recommended latency-safe fallback models? like moving from 13B to 7B in overload?
[14:36] Ethan: yes: route non-critical requests to a cheaper 7B quantized variant; Redwood's routing can downgrade for cost/latency and optionally rerank outputs through the larger model for quality-sensitive paths. This hybrid reduces p95 without losing entirely on quality.
[14:58] Alex: how about a practical pilot?
[15:02] Maya: proposal: 1-week pilot inside your VPC: wire up telemetry, run 2 reserved GPUs sized for baseline, configure warm standby 1 node, enable burst to 6 nodes, and run synthetic traffic + a shadow of real traffic. Redwood provides bench scripts and we'll run a capacity plan report at end.
[15:22] Alex: sounds good. what's the onboarding time?
[15:25] Ethan: with our Private package and pre-validated AMIs it's 3-5 business days to stand up the control plane and initial nodes, assuming network approvals go quickly.
[15:36] [16:00] Priya: what data we need to share?
[16:03] Maya: traces (RPS by route, token distributions, session stickiness), allowed network egress rules, and KMS ARN if you're using that. We'll provide a checklist.
[16:15] Alex: we'll get traces by Friday.
[16:18] Daniel: one more thing - can we do a stretch test of cold-starts? we want to validate the 10-45s range you mentioned.
[16:24] Ethan: yes, we'll include cold-start bench with both pre-pulled images and without, across your on-prem hardware profile.
[16:32] [17:00] Maya: wrapping up, summary of decisions: pilot with 2 reserved GPUs, 1 warm standby, burst to 6 nodes; share traces; Redwood to send bench configs, security docs, pricing draft.
[17:12] Alex: agreed.
[17:15] Priya: agreed.
[17:18] Daniel: thanks, will review the docs.
[17:21] [17:30] Maya: action items we'll capture and send. thanks all.
